excerpts.text: **Editorial interpretation:** the general object to pull back is \(L\psi^*(e_*\tau[-g])\), with the zero-section pushforward included; its omission from the first displayed corollary cannot be resolved by erasing the derived geometry. When \(\psi\) is flat, this becomes \(\mathcal O_K\otimes_S\tau[-g]\), and regularity of the pulled-back zero section explains perfection of \(\mathcal O_K\). For a nonflat \(\psi\), the derived inverse image can retain higher Tor, so an ordinary structure sheaf need not suffice. **Confidence: high**, because the distinction follows from flat base change and the same local Koszul calculation as item F8.

excerpts.heading: R9 — Unpursued implication: identify the cited injective-module results precisely
excerpts.text: The decomposition and filtration statements have direct counterparts in Matlis (1958, Theorem 2.5, Proposition 3.1, and Theorem 3.10): the last result identifies the successive annihilator quotients with duals of the corresponding graded pieces of the maximal ideal after localization. This supplies a precise reference for the displayed dimension equality without identifying the reused typescript's author or date. In particular, uniqueness here is uniqueness of the isomorphism classes and multiplicities of summands, not a canonical choice of embedded summands; the latter distinction matters when using this decomposition to construct sheaves.

excerpts.heading: R10 — Own idea: isolate the adjunction in the injective-sheaf argument
excerpts.text: Since taking a stalk is exact, the right side is exact contravariantly in \(F\), proving that \(i_{x*}I\) is injective among all \(\mathcal O_X\)-modules. For the particular injective hull \(I=E(k(\mathfrak p))\) used on the page, the distinct geometric step is the identification \(\widetilde I\simeq i_{x*}I\): the displayed filtration reduces it to modules annihilated by powers of \(\mathfrak p\), for which localization is zero when the inverted element belongs to \(\mathfrak p\) and is an isomorphism when it does not. This separates the general adjunction argument from the noetherian algebra needed to establish that identification.

excerpts.heading: F14 — Cote 47, scan 9, final integrality claim
excerpts.text: **Editorial distinction:** with the corrected \(c_k\), the coefficient asserted integral at the foot of the page equals \((-1)^k r\,c_k(E)\), rather than \(c_k(E)\) itself. Thus the numerical error in the expansion does not refute that weaker integrality consequence in the ample situation of item F11, where the actual Chern classes provide integral algebraic lifts. Equality after tensoring Chow groups with \(\mathbf Q\), membership in the image of integral cycles, and a torsion-sensitive equality in \(K\)-theory or in a specified filtration are different assertions. **Confidence: high**, because the coefficient comparison is exact; extension beyond the stated geometric case remains conditional.

Autre question de terminologie : le Congrès avait adopté d'enthousiasme une belle terminologie symétrique : ``poids'', ``poids radiciels'', ``copoids'', ``copoids radiciels''. Le malheur est qu'avec la définition adoptée, un ``copoids radiciel'' \uline{n'est pas} nécessairement un ``copoids'', ce qui est grammaticalement intolérable. Le rédacteur voit trois solutions possibles :

1) Prendre une autre terminologie pour ``poids radiciels'' et ``copoids radiciels'' ; c'est la solution adoptée dans la rédaction, qui dit respectivement ``vocables'' et ``covocables'', (dactylo, attention, ce n'est \uline{pas} ``convocables''!). Le rédacteur ne tient pas spécialement à ces termes ; on pourrait aussi dire ``noeuds'' et ``conoeuds'' bien que ce dernier mot ait l'air un peu ... ce que vous pensez.

2) On ne peut naturellement changer le sens reçu de ``racines'' et ``poids'' ; mais ``copoids'' est beaucoup plus récent, (Chevalley, je crois), et pas encore très répandu ; on pourrait donc intervertir les sens de ``copoids'' et ``copoids radiciels'', les poids étant donc associés aux copoids radiciels, (et non plus aux copoids), et les copoids radiciels étant engendrés par les coracines, (ce qui est assez satisfaisant).

3) N'utiliser aucune terminologie pour ``poids radiciels'' et ``copoids radiciels'' ; l'expérience, (tout au moins dans la présente rédaction), montre qu'on s'en sert en fait très peu et qu'on s'en passe fort bien.

excerpts.text: ### S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite

excerpts.heading: S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
excerpts.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

excerpts.heading: S17 — Finite-field Künneth projectors illustrate a narrower later result
excerpts.text: For smooth projective varieties over finite fields, Katz and Messing (1974, Theorem 2) construct rational algebraic Künneth projectors as rational combinations of graphs of Frobenius iterates, compatibly with the cohomology theories in their hypotheses. Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

excerpts.heading: Abstract Lefschetz algebra and standard conjectures
excerpts.text: This supplement concerns the frozen transcription of cote 16; scan numbers, rather than reconstructed chronology, identify the evidence. The propositions discussed below concern smooth projective varieties, rational algebraic correspondence classes, and a fixed cohomology theory unless another setting is expressly stated. “Editorial” marks an independent calculation or proposed interpretation, not a completion silently inserted into the manuscript; no claim of novelty or priority is made. The written parameter remains uncertain between \(\ell\) and \(\chi\), although \(\ell\) is used provisionally in this commentary.

excerpts.heading: S7 — Hard Lefschetz supplies linear inverses, not their cycles
excerpts.text: Deligne (1980, Theorem 4.1.1) proves hard Lefschetz for an ample class on a smooth projective variety over an algebraically closed field, with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-coefficients and \(\ell\) different from the characteristic: \(L^{n-i}:H^i\to H^{2n-i}\) is an isomorphism. Applied to the draft, this settles the existence of the indicated cohomological inverses in that setting, while the additional demand that an inverse arise from a rational algebraic correspondence remains a separate assertion. Keeping these two steps explicit also prevents the later theorem from concealing the integral obstruction in scan 14, where the coefficient ring is \(\mathbb Z\).

excerpts.heading: S17 — Finite-field Künneth projectors illustrate a narrower later result
excerpts.text: For smooth projective varieties over finite fields, Katz and Messing (1974, Theorem 2) construct rational algebraic Künneth projectors as rational combinations of graphs of Frobenius iterates, compatibly with the cohomology theories in their hypotheses. Their theorem also gives integral, theory-independent characteristic polynomials for integral degree-zero correspondences. These results strengthen two particular ingredients appearing in the letters, but the projector statement is published condition \(C\), not the draft's stronger inverse-operator condition \(C_\ell\). Moreover, rationality in the Cayley–Hamilton criterion still has to be coupled with the required algebraic complementary-degree isomorphisms.

excerpts.heading: S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
excerpts.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

excerpts.heading: S15 — Numerical motives have a later unconditional theorem
excerpts.text: Jannsen (1992, Theorem 1) proves, for characteristic-zero coefficient fields and adequate equivalence relations, that the category of pure motives is semisimple abelian precisely when the equivalence relation is numerical. Thus numerical motives provide a later unconditional realization of the broad semisimplicity goal, without assuming the standard conjectures. The manuscript's actual operators, however, act on a chosen cohomology theory and are taken modulo homological equivalence, so transferring the conclusion to that category requires identifying the relevant equivalence relations. Quotienting by numerical equivalence changes the problem unless that identification has been established.

excerpts.heading: S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
excerpts.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

excerpts.heading: S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
excerpts.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

excerpts.heading: S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
excerpts.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

excerpts.heading: F3 — Cote 47, scans 4–6, inversion theorem and anti-diagonal kernel

excerpts.heading: R17 — Unpursued implication: the proposed nilpotent appendix is a categorical statement
excerpts.text: Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). For the proposed appendix, one must prove both lifting of finite étale algebras and unique lifting of their morphisms; existence of lifted defining equations alone proves neither the full equivalence nor its functoriality. The statement concerns the category of covers, and is compatible with the underlying scheme retaining its nilpotent structure.

excerpts.heading: R17 — Unpursued implication: the proposed nilpotent appendix is a categorical statement
excerpts.text: Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). For the proposed appendix, one must prove both lifting of finite étale algebras and unique lifting of their morphisms; existence of lifted defining equations alone proves neither the full equivalence nor its functoriality. The statement concerns the category of covers, and is compatible with the underlying scheme retaining its nilpotent structure.

excerpts.text: ## Fourier transforms, determinant lines, and Chern coefficients

excerpts.heading: F15 — Cote 47, scan 9, question about torsion
excerpts.text: A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms. These additional hypotheses and the distinction between rational identities and integral lifts prevent the manuscript’s local heuristic from being treated as a general integral-transform theorem.

excerpts.heading: F3 — Cote 47, scans 4–6, inversion theorem and anti-diagonal kernel
excerpts.text: The composition kernel is governed by the classifying map \((a_1,a_2)\mapsto a_1+a_2\), so its zero locus is the graph of inversion. Mukai’s field-case inversion theorem gives the corresponding equivalence with composite \((-1_A)^*[-g]\) (Mukai, 1981, Theorem 2.2), and the relative line factor is addressed in item F4. The manuscript’s proof is therefore organized around the appropriate kernel, but scan 5 still retains an earlier target “\(\simeq\operatorname{id}\)” after the theorem above it has been corrected.

excerpts.heading: R12 — Unproved claim: a later compatibility check remains explicitly unfinished
excerpts.text: The published continuation asks for compatibility between the discriminant pairing and the cohomological construction, and Remark 8.5 acknowledges that this verification has not been carried out (Grothendieck, 1968, pp. 150–151). Thus the elementary matrix calculation in R4 does not by itself establish that compatibility. A reconstruction must compare the cycle class, Kummer boundary, cup product, and local trace maps with their signs, rather than merely exhibit two perfect pairings on abstractly isomorphic finite groups.

excerpts.heading: 16:17:6 — unpursued implication
excerpts.text: The required datum is an operator together with a prescribed grading, which is stricter than a bare nilpotent or raising operator. Comparing the resulting moduli of representations with the moduli obtained after forgetting the grading could clarify the role of the extra hypothesis added on scan16.

excerpts.text: The proposed appendix states invariance of finite étale algebras under a nilpotent thickening A→A/I and points to S. G. A. A proof would establish both lifting of objects and unique lifting of morphisms, yielding an equivalence of categories rather than only a bijection on isomorphism classes.

excerpts.heading: R17 — Unpursued implication: the proposed nilpotent appendix is a categorical statement
excerpts.text: Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). For the proposed appendix, one must prove both lifting of finite étale algebras and unique lifting of their morphisms; existence of lifted defining equations alone proves neither the full equivalence nor its functoriality. The statement concerns the category of covers, and is compatible with the underlying scheme retaining its nilpotent structure.

excerpts.text: For an abelian variety $A$ with dual $B$, the comparison identifies $\operatorname{Lie}E(A)$ with $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(B)$, whereas invariant differentials on $E(A)$ identify with $H^1_{\mathrm{dR}}(A)$; confusing these two statements reverses the variance (Coleman, 1998, §§2, 4).

excerpts.heading: R17 — Unpursued implication: the proposed nilpotent appendix is a categorical statement
excerpts.text: Finite étale covers are indeed invariant under nilpotent thickenings, and the modern statement allows arbitrary thickenings of schemes (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BQB, Lemma 58.8.3). For the proposed appendix, one must prove both lifting of finite étale algebras and unique lifting of their morphisms; existence of lifted defining equations alone proves neither the full equivalence nor its functoriality. The statement concerns the category of covers, and is compatible with the underlying scheme retaining its nilpotent structure.

excerpts.heading: S13 — Positivity kills the radical once the rational algebra is finite
excerpts.text: Let a finite-dimensional rational algebra \(R\) have a faithful finite-dimensional realization, an involution \(*\), a rational-valued trace, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(x^*x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in R\); its Jacobson radical is involution-stable and nilpotent, so \(x^*x\) has trace zero for \(x\) in the radical, forcing that radical to vanish. Finite dimension over \(\mathbb Q\) should not be inferred merely from inclusion in matrices over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); however, a rational positive trace pairing bounds the size of any rationally independent family by the ambient matrix dimension, since its Gram determinant is nonzero. This supplies the elementary algebra after the geometric work has produced the appropriate adjoint and rational positive pairing. Kleiman (1968, §§3.11–3.14) establishes the conditional positivity, semisimplicity, and splitting route.

Soit $\mathcal C$ une catégorie additive $^{(*)}$. Le \uline{groupe de Grothendieck} $K(\mathcal C)$ de la catégorie $\mathcal C$ est le quotient du groupe libre engendré par les classes d'isomorphie $\{G\}$ d'objets $G$ de $\mathcal C$ par le sous-groupe engendré par les relations $\{E+F\}-\{E\}-\{F\}=0$. Pour des applications topologiques du groupe de Grothendieck, voir par exemple $^{(1)}$. Dans cette note on se propose de définir de même, pour des catégories additives munies d'une certaine structure, des groupes $K^n(\mathcal C)$, $n\in Z$, avec $K^0(\mathcal C)\approx K(\mathcal C)$, jouissant de certaines propriétés ``cohomologiques'' en relation avec les théorèmes de périodicité de Bott.

excerpts.heading: S14 — An injective map needs an algebraic splitting
excerpts.text: The previous isomorphism argument cannot simply be applied to an injection between spaces of different dimensions, because no inverse exists on the whole target. If the correspondence algebra of the direct sum of source and target, with the required Tate twist, is semisimple, its matrix-block structure gives a generalized inverse \(g\) with \(fgf=f\), and injectivity of the realized \(f\) then yields \(gf=1\) on the source. The corner containing \(g\) is the required algebraic left inverse; surjections are treated with the opposite equation. This pinpoints why information about the ambient correspondence algebra and its products is needed, whereas semisimplicity of an isolated endomorphism algebra would not by itself control all maps between two varieties.

Soit $\mathcal C$ une catégorie additive $^{(*)}$. Le \uline{groupe de Grothendieck} $K(\mathcal C)$ de la catégorie $\mathcal C$ est le quotient du groupe libre engendré par les classes d'isomorphie $\{G\}$ d'objets $G$ de $\mathcal C$ par le sous-groupe engendré par les relations $\{E+F\}-\{E\}-\{F\}=0$. Pour des applications topologiques du groupe de Grothendieck, voir par exemple $^{(1)}$. Dans cette note on se propose de définir de même, pour des catégories additives munies d'une certaine structure, des groupes $K^n(\mathcal C)$, $n\in Z$, avec $K^0(\mathcal C)\approx K(\mathcal C)$, jouissant de certaines propriétés ``cohomologiques'' en relation avec les théorèmes de périodicité de Bott.

Soit $\mathcal C$ une catégorie additive $^{(*)}$. excerpts.heading: R16 — Unproved claim: trace duality needs its own assumptions
excerpts.text: The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

excerpts.text: - **62** scans 2-50: "Courbes elliptiques (généralités - vieille rédaction) : notes manuscrites (s.d.)." ([à partir de 1963][53]). Book I, I.VIII Chapter VIII: Picard schemes, Jacobians, abelian schemes, elliptic curves; rank 23.

Le rédacteur a suivi aussi fidèlement que possible les instructions de La Tribu n$^{\mathrm{o}}$ 57. Le plan n'a été modifié qu'en ce qui concerne les remords-fourre-tout du début, que le rédacteur a jugé préférable de grouper en 3 paragraphes préliminaires au lieu d'un, le 3e étant consacré aux lemmes sur les graphes qui traînaient un peu partout, et dont en fait on a besoin dès le début, (p. ex. pour le critère pour qu'une matrice de Coxeter soit connexe). Conformément aux injonctions de La Tribu, le rédacteur a suivi la terminologie de Berge pour les graphes ; mais si les termes de ``sommet'' et ``arête'' sont classiques, le rédacteur n'aime guère ``sommet pendant'' qui a l'air grotesque, et préférerait ``point d'arrêt'', qui irait assez bien avec ``point de ramification''.

Autre question de terminologie : le Congrès avait adopté d'enthousiasme une belle terminologie symétrique : ``poids'', ``poids radiciels'', ``copoids'', ``copoids radiciels''. Le malheur est qu'avec la définition adoptée, un ``copoids radiciel'' \uline{n'est pas} nécessairement un ``copoids'', ce qui est grammaticalement intolérable. Le rédacteur voit trois solutions possibles :

1) Prendre une autre terminologie pour ``poids radiciels'' et ``copoids radiciels'' ; c'est la solution adoptée dans la rédaction, qui dit respectivement ``vocables'' et ``covocables'', (dactylo, attention, ce n'est \uline{pas} ``convocables''!). Le rédacteur ne tient pas spécialement à ces termes ; on pourrait aussi dire ``noeuds'' et ``conoeuds'' bien que ce dernier mot ait l'air un peu ... ce que vous pensez.

3) N'utiliser aucune terminologie pour ``poids radiciels'' et ``copoids radiciels'' ; l'expérience, (tout au moins dans la présente rédaction), montre qu'on s'en sert en fait très peu et qu'on s'en passe fort bien.

excerpts.text: The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

excerpts.heading: R16 — Unproved claim: trace duality needs its own assumptions
excerpts.text: The trace construction uses a complementary module \(\{x:\operatorname{Tr}(xB)\subset A\}\) in a generically étale total quotient algebra, whereas the Kähler construction uses a presentation of differentials; their definitions should not be identified before proving a comparison (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tags 0BW0 and 0BTC, §§49.8–49.9). The page's proposed discrete-valuation comparison therefore calls for an explicit account of finiteness, the generic separability assumption, and the relationship between the trace module and the local complete-intersection presentation. A modern dualizing-module formulation also supplies a composition map for quasi-finite noetherian ring maps, but the existence of that map alone is weaker than the transitivity equality sought here (The Stacks Project Authors, 2026, Tag 0BT4, Lemma 49.2.6).

excerpts.heading: F9 — Cote 47, scan 6, general corollary and flat-epimorphism specialization
excerpts.text: **Editorial interpretation:** the general object to pull back is \(L\psi^*(e_*\tau[-g])\), with the zero-section pushforward included; its omission from the first displayed corollary cannot be resolved by erasing the derived geometry. When \(\psi\) is flat, this becomes \(\mathcal O_K\otimes_S\tau[-g]\), and regularity of the pulled-back zero section explains perfection of \(\mathcal O_K\). For a nonflat \(\psi\), the derived inverse image can retain higher Tor, so an ordinary structure sheaf need not suffice. **Confidence: high**, because the distinction follows from flat base change and the same local Koszul calculation as item F8.

excerpts.text: ## Fourier transforms, determinant lines, and Chern coefficients

excerpts.heading: F15 — Cote 47, scan 9, question about torsion
excerpts.text: A useful later comparison distinguishes a particular bundle’s integral Chern classes from an integral Fourier transform on the entire Chow group. Beckmann and de Gaay Fortman (2023, Theorem 3.8) characterize integral lifts of the Poincaré character using a specific one-cycle; under a symmetric ample principal polarization, they also relate this to preservation of Chow groups modulo torsion and to weak integral Fourier transforms. These additional hypotheses and the distinction between rational identities and integral lifts prevent the manuscript’s local heuristic from being treated as a general integral-transform theorem.
